# Threshold

**Exposure therapy on a live world.** The thing you're scared of becomes a live scene, generated by Visko Orbis in real time. Your therapist steers it while you watch. It gets harder as you settle and easier the second you need it.

Built for the Visko Orbis Online Challenge, on top of the Reactor hackathon starter.

## Overview

Exposure therapy is the treatment that works best for phobias, and most therapists never do it, because you can't book a lecture hall every week and you can't tell a real crowd to calm down when a patient panics. VR was supposed to fix that, but the scenes come from a fixed library. You pick a clip from a menu.

Threshold gives the therapist a dial instead. A session has two screens:

- **The patient screen** streams the scene from Orbis over WebRTC, shows a 0 to 100 anxiety slider (the scale therapists already use) and one button, Safe place.
- **The therapist console** sees and hears the same stream, relayed live, and runs the room: a ladder of steps for the fear, a box to type anything, interruptions, a camera pull back, a restart, a live anxiety chart and a report at the end.

Every step is one sentence sent to Orbis. About four seconds later the room has changed, and it's still the same room.

## The seven fears

| Fear | Scene | Steps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public speaking | An auditorium seen from the lectern | 8 |
| Heights | The open edge of a skyscraper roof, a beam over the drop | 7 |
| Flying | A window seat at cruising altitude | 6 |
| The dark | A house hallway at night, a door ajar at the far end | 7 |
| Asking someone out | Across a cafe table | 7 |
| Spiders | A tarantula on your desk | 7 |
| Small spaces | An old elevator | 7 |

Every step was checked on a live stream. The ones that didn't show up on screen were replaced with ones that did. The full list is in `lib/threshold/ladders.ts`, with the reasons in the comments.

## Getting started

You need Node.js 20.9 or newer and a Reactor API key with access to Visko Orbis Stable.

```bash
git clone <this repo>
cd orbis-online-hackathon-starter
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local
```

Put your key in `.env.local`:

```dotenv
REACTOR_API_KEY=your_reactor_api_key
```

Then run it:

```bash
npm run dev
```

Open <http://localhost:3000>.

The key stays on the server. The browser only ever gets a short lived Reactor token, minted by `app/api/token/route.ts`. Each token allows one session of up to 15 minutes.

`npm run dev` goes through a small wrapper from the starter that records dev sessions in a gitignored file and deletes them before startup and on Ctrl+C, so a restart can't leave an Orbis session running and burning credits.

## Running a session

1. On the home page pick a fear and click **Create a session**. You get a four letter code and two links.
2. Open the **Patient** link on the screen the patient will watch and click **Begin session**. Orbis takes about ten seconds to start.
3. Open the **Clinician** link on the other screen. It connects to the same code, shows the patient's stream and the console.
4. The patient moves the slider as they feel. The therapist clicks a step on the ladder, types a direction, or turns on **Adapt automatically** to follow the habituation rule (hold a step until anxiety drops to half its peak, then go up; above 85, ease off).
5. **Safe place** on either screen backs the room off in one step. **End session** shows the report on both screens.

Solo mode, one screen with the console beside the scene: `http://localhost:3000/session?fear=horror` (any ladder id from `lib/threshold/ladders.ts`). Add `&live=0` to run the whole UI on saved frames without spending credits.

## How it works

**The world.** Each fear is one sentence that already has the scary thing in it, plus a camera line. Orbis generated it once, we kept the first clean frame, and that frame anchors every session after. It's what keeps the scene consistent and lets us restart it. Anchors live in `public/anchors/`.

**The ladder.** Each step is one action, about a dozen words, about things already on screen. Moving to a step is a single `set_prompt`. Going back down starts with how the current step ends ("The laughter stops."). Sound is only prompted for steps that are a sound.

**The engine.** A small state machine in `lib/threshold/engine.ts` that watches the ratings and applies the habituation rule. It's off by default; the therapist drives.

**The two screens.** Next.js and React. The patient page streams Orbis through Reactor's SDK and posts its state every second. The server holds a room per code and a numbered list of commands, so a click can't get lost even if the console reloads. The console polls that, sends commands, and receives a browser to browser WebRTC relay of the patient's stream. Orbis streams once, so a shared session costs the same as a solo one.

```
app/
  page.tsx                 intake: pick a fear, create a session
  session/                 solo mode
  patient/                 patient screen (shared)
  therapist/               therapist console (shared)
  api/token/               mints the Reactor token
  api/room/[code]/         room state, commands, relay signalling
components/threshold/      session view, console, report, chart
hooks/
  use-orbis-session.ts     Reactor SDK: connect, start, prompts
  use-threshold-session.ts the session: ladder, engine, log
  use-room-sync.ts         patient side of a shared session
lib/threshold/
  ladders.ts               the seven fears, step by step
  director.ts              turns a jump into the one prompt Orbis needs
  engine.ts                the habituation rule
  protocol.ts, rtc.ts      shared session messages and the relay
lib/server/room-store.ts   in memory rooms
public/anchors/            the first frame of every scene, plus reference frames
```

## What Orbis taught us

Most of the work was finding out how Orbis reads a prompt. It takes everything literally.

- Say "the camera" and it moves the camera. Say "the speaker" and it puts a speaker on stage. Even saying where the audience is looking makes it invent someone to look at.
- Name one person and it zooms in on them and stays there. Steps act on the crowd or the room; one named person only for the climax.
- Lighting and colour always show. So do things that fill the frame: smoke, water, oxygen masks, a crowd laughing. Small things (a trembling flashlight beam, a shadow, fog) don't.
- A horror figure needs a full description. "A tall figure" is a man in a coat.
- After five or six prompts the view starts to wander. The console has **Pull back** and **Restart scene** for that.

## Troubleshooting

- **Nothing changes after a click.** Changes land at the next chunk, about four seconds. Prompts are never sent closer together than that.
- **The camera has wandered off.** Click **Pull back**, or **Restart scene** to rebuild from the anchor at the current step. Faces will change.
- **Someone appeared who shouldn't be there.** Restart scene. And don't say where people are looking.
- **The stream ended on its own.** Sessions are capped at 15 minutes per token. End and begin again.
- **Two screens don't connect.** Both need the same code, and the patient must have clicked Begin session first.

## What's next

A pilot with a university counselling service. Letting a therapist write a new fear from a sentence. Heart rate input so the room can react without a slider. A history across sessions, so progress shows over weeks and not just one sitting.

## Built with

Visko Orbis through Reactor, Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, WebRTC, Zustand.

Starter code from the Reactor Orbis hackathon starter, which this repo is forked from.
